messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Henry, a 77-year-old delivery driver from a small town in North America, had always prided himself on being reliable and hardworking. For decades, he had navigated his routes with a sense of purpose, delivering goods and smiles to his customers. However, ever since the assault that occurred two years ago, his life had taken a turn he never anticipated. 

On a chilly evening, Henry had stopped to make a routine delivery at a local convenience store. As he stepped out of his truck, he was startled by a sudden confrontation. A group of young men approached him aggressively, demanding money. In that moment, Henry felt a surge of fear unlike any he had ever experienced. He remembered their harsh voices and the way they closed in on him, their intentions clear and violent. He had tried to reason with them, but the encounter escalated quickly. One of them struck him, and the pain of the blow was sharp, but what lingered longer was the fear that gripped him. It was not just about the physical pain; it was the realization that he could be vulnerable and powerless at his age.

In the months that followed, Henry found himself wrestling with a barrage of feelings that he struggled to articulate. When he sat down with his wife, Margaret, for dinner, he often felt a tight knot in his stomach. He would chew his food slowly, aware of the way his heart raced whenever he thought about the assault. To manage this distress, he began to overeat, believing that filling his stomach would somehow fill the void of the fear that had taken hold of him. Margaret noticed the way he would pile his plate high, almost as if he were trying to shield himself from the feelings that threatened to drown him. But instead of feeling better, he only felt more trapped in a cycle he couldn’t escape.

As the days turned into weeks, Henry adopted another strategy: he kept himself busy. He took on extra delivery routes, working late into the night. While his colleagues joked about the long hours, Henry felt a sense of relief in the chaos of his job. If he focused on the deliveries, the customers, the endless paperwork, he could avoid thinking about that night. He thought that if he kept moving, he could outrun the memories that haunted him. But the more he worked, the less connected he felt to his family. Margaret would often sit in silence, longing for the husband she once knew, while Henry was consumed with the need to stay busy, as if busyness were his only salvation.

Yet, when he did pause, the thoughts came rushing back. Henry tried hard to suppress them, convinced that if he allowed himself to think about the event, he would crumble under the weight of it. He felt he could not trust himself to handle the emotions that followed; the belief that he would be unable to cope spiraled into a deep sense of self-doubt. “What if I break down?” he would think, replaying the assault in his mind. “What if I can’t go back to work? I can’t let that happen.” 

These thoughts shattered the beliefs Henry had held about the world being a safe place. He had always believed that hard work and honesty would protect him, but that night had dismantled those convictions. Now, he walked through life with a constant undercurrent of anxiety, feeling as though the world was a dangerous place filled with people who could turn violent at any moment. 

Despite the toll it took on him, Henry continued to avoid talking about the assault, even with Margaret. He didn’t want to burden her with the darkness that had enveloped him. But as time went on, he could see the concern in her eyes. He noticed how she would gently touch his arm, urging him to share his feelings, but each time he would shake his head, suppressing the urge to voice the turmoil inside. 

It wasn’t until last week, after a particularly long day filled with dread and an overwhelming sense of isolation, that Henry finally reached a breaking point. While delivering to a familiar store, the sight of a group of young men loitering outside sent him into a panic, and he found himself frozen in place, his chest tightening with fear. The memory of his assault crashed over him like a wave, and for the first time, he felt the weight of its impact too heavy to bear alone. 

That evening, he sat down with Margaret and, through tears, revealed his struggles for the first time. “I don’t know how to handle this,” he admitted, the words tumbling out. He felt vulnerable, yet there was a glimmer of hope in seeking help. Now, as he contemplates the future, Henry is filled with a mix of fear and hope. He wonders if he can reclaim his life, if it’s possible to trust himself again, and whether he can find a way to feel safe in the world after all that had happened.
